reference_title: California Trenching and Shoring Manual (Caltrans, June 2011, Revision 2 - July 2025)

sections.title: Allowable Working Stresses (Timber and Steel)
sections.summary: Structure Construction reviews trenching and shoring by Allowable Stress Design (ASD). Timber: reference the Falsework Manual, Chapter 5, Analysis; the current NDS is used for timber connections (Section 6-1). Shoring adjacent to railroads is designed and reviewed to the railroad's requirements (Guidelines for Temporary Shoring, based primarily on AREMA Chapter 7, Timber Structures; Chapter 9 of this manual). Steel: assume ASTM A36 unless identified; allowable stress must not exceed the current AISC Steel Construction Manual limit; compression members as pinned-end columns; large point loads reviewed for web yielding and crippling.
sections.body: It is Structure Construction practice to review trenching and shoring by Allowable Stress Design (ASD), as specified in the Standard Specifications for falsework design and the AREMA Manual for Railway Engineering (Section 6-1). For aluminum and concrete members use the latest acceptable national standard; for timber connections use the current National Design Specification for Wood Construction (NDS) (Section 6-1). Timber (6-2.01): for timber shoring analysis, reference the Falsework Manual, Chapter 5, Analysis, for guidance on allowable working stress values. Shoring adjacent to railroads is to be designed and reviewed in accordance with railroad requirements, found in the railroad's Guidelines for Temporary Shoring, which is based primarily on the AREMA manual, Chapter 7, Timber Structures, Appendix 4, Temporary Structures; Chapter 9, Railroads, of this manual gives additional details. Cal/OSHA CSO 1541.1 Appendix C defines minimum timber member sizes (uprights, walers, cross bracing) for excavations not exceeding 20 ft in depth and only with the minimum surcharge; member substitutions require manufactured members of equivalent strength (Appendix E shows some alternatives). Steel (6-2.02): unless otherwise identified, assume ASTM Grade A36; the maximum allowable stress for an identified grade must not exceed the limit in the current AISC Steel Construction Manual. When lagging is placed against the front flange of W or HP sections, the entire length may be assumed laterally supported for compression-flange buckling (the best practice for placement of lagging); lagging on the back side requires a compression-flange-buckling check, and Fb could be reduced significantly (compact / non-compact / partially compact). For steel members (excluding sheet piles) use the ASD requirements of the AISC manual: (1) check the Contractor's system against the steel standard the Contractor is using; (2) members strictly in compression: allowable axial stress per AISC with pinned ends; (3) elements carrying large point loads should be reviewed for web yielding and web crippling (Falsework Manual 5-4.07, 5-4.08; AISC J10); (4) bolted connections per the most current AISC manual. Railroads have different allowable stress requirements; see Chapter 9, Railroad.
key_points: Shoring is reviewed by Allowable Stress Design (ASD)
Timber: reference the Falsework Manual, Chapter 5, Analysis; timber connections per the current NDS
Steel: assume ASTM A36 unless identified; allowable stress not to exceed the current AISC Steel Construction Manual
Compression members checked as pinned-end columns; large point loads reviewed for web yielding/crippling
Railroad shoring: the railroad's Guidelines for Temporary Shoring (AREMA Chapter 7, Timber Structures); see Chapter 9

sections.title: Overstress
sections.summary: Short-term increases to allowable stresses are permitted up to 133 percent (a 1.33 factor), EXCEPT when the excavation is in place more than 90 days, dynamic loadings are present (pile driving, traffic), the excavation is adjacent to railroads, or horizontal struts are being analyzed.
sections.body: Short-term increases to allowable stresses are allowed (to a maximum of 133 percent) except in the following situations when: (1) excavations are in place more than 90 days; (2) dynamic loadings are present (pile driving, traffic, etc.); (3) excavations are adjacent to railroads; (4) analyzing horizontal struts.
key_points: Short-term increases to allowable stresses are allowed to a maximum of 133%
Not allowed for excavations in place more than 90 days
Not allowed where dynamic loadings are present (pile driving, traffic, etc.)
Not allowed for excavations adjacent to railroads or when analyzing horizontal struts

equations.description: Short-term allowable-stress increase up to 1.33 (133%), with four exceptions.

sections.applicability: Deciding whether the 133% short-term overstress increase may be used in a shoring check

sections.title: Lagging
sections.summary: Soil arching redistributes pressure from the lagging center to the stiffer soldier piles, so the design load on the lagging may be taken as 0.6 times the calculated earth pressure; studies have shown a maximum lagging pressure of 400 psf should be expected when surcharges are not affecting the system. Without soil arching, reduced lagging loads should not be considered. Table 6-2 (FHWA) gives minimum rough-cut timber lagging thicknesses by soil group and clear span where arching can develop; it should not be used adjacent to existing facilities, including railroads, and lagging with surcharges is analyzed separately.
sections.body: Lagging is placed between the flanges of W or HP piles; installing lagging behind the back flange is not recommended because the arching action of the supported soil will be destroyed and the compression flange's unsupported length affected. Voids behind lagging should be filled with compacted material; lagging may be spaced up to 1-1/2 inches apart to permit seepage. For the arching effect to occur, the backside of the soldier pile must bear against the soil (Figure 6-1). Lateral soil movement within the failure wedge induces soil arching behind the lagging, redistributing pressure away from the lagging center toward the much stiffer soldier-pile support. Because of this, the design load on the lagging may be taken as 0.6 times the theoretical or calculated earth pressure (lagging design load = 0.6 (shoring design load)). Studies have shown that a maximum lagging pressure of 400 psf should be expected when surcharges are not affecting the system (maximum lagging load may be 400 psf when no surcharges are present). Without soil arching, the pressure redistribution would not occur, and reduced lagging loads should not be considered. Lagging stress analysis follows Falsework Manual Section 5-2, Timber Members. Table 6-2 lists FHWA recommended minimum thicknesses of construction grade rough cut Douglas fir lagging for Competent, Difficult and Potentially Dangerous soils (for the last, the appropriateness of lagging is questionable) by depth and clear span. The tabular values may be used where soil arching behind the lagging can develop; they should not be used for excavations adjacent to existing facilities, including railroads. Analyze the lagging used in conjunction with surcharges separately.
key_points: Lagging design load = 0.6 * calculated earth pressure (soil arching reduction)
Maximum lagging load may be 400 psf when no surcharges are present
Without soil arching, reduced lagging loads should not be considered
Analyze surcharge effects on lagging separately
Table 6-2 (FHWA) lagging thicknesses: where arching can develop; not for excavations adjacent to existing facilities, including railroads

equations.description: Lagging design load = 0.6 (shoring design load) where soil arching develops; maximum lagging load may be 400 psf when no surcharges are present.
